questions.title: Write typed utilities: DeepPartial, groupBy and debounce
questions.quick: I would write three small, strictly typed helpers. DeepPartial is a recursive conditional mapped type that leaves functions alone and maps arrays element-wise. groupBy takes a key selector and returns a Record keyed by the selector's return type, using nullish assignment to create buckets. Debounce preserves the argument tuple with a generic rest parameter, stores the timer as ReturnType of setTimeout so it works in Node and browsers, and exposes cancel. I would then test the runtime pieces with fake timers.
questions.revision: DeepPartial recurses through objects and arrays; groupBy buckets by a typed key function; debounce preserves argument types with a generic tuple and exposes cancel.
followUps: How would you test the type of `DeepPartial` itself?
Why not use `Object.groupBy`, and which runtimes support it?
How does debounce differ from throttle?

questions.title: Wrap an async call with a timeout and AbortController in Node
questions.quick: I would write withTimeout that hands the task an AbortSignal, races it against a timer, and aborts the signal when the deadline passes so the underlying request actually stops. A parent signal can also cancel it. I use a dedicated TimeoutError, always clear the timer and remove listeners in finally, and never rely on the race alone because a promise that loses the race keeps running unless it honours the signal.
questions.revision: Race the task against a timer, abort a controller on timeout so work really stops, support a parent signal, and clean up timer and listeners in finally.
followUps: What is the difference between a timeout and cancellation?
Why does the process stay alive if the timer is not cleared?
What happens to the underlying TCP connection after abort?

questions.title: Express middleware for correlation IDs and structured request logging
questions.quick: I would add two middlewares. The first accepts an incoming correlation header only if it matches a safe pattern, otherwise generates a UUID, echoes it on the response and stores it in AsyncLocalStorage so any logger deeper in the stack can read it. The second records start time and, on the response finish event, emits one structured JSON line with method, route template, status and duration. I would log the route pattern rather than the raw URL to keep cardinality low and avoid leaking identifiers.
questions.revision: Validate or generate a correlation ID, store it in AsyncLocalStorage, echo it, and log one structured line per request on response finish with route template and duration.
followUps: Why AsyncLocalStorage instead of attaching to `req`?
What is the performance cost of AsyncLocalStorage?
How do you correlate logs across a queue consumer?

questions.title: Implement validated cursor pagination for a list endpoint
questions.quick: I would use keyset pagination on a stable sort of createdAt then id, both descending. The query string is validated with a schema: limit is coerced, bounded and defaulted. The cursor is an opaque base64url encoding of the last item's sort keys, decoded and validated defensively so tampering gives a 400. I fetch limit plus one rows to know whether there is a next page, trim the extra, and return items with a nextCursor or null. This stays fast on deep pages, unlike offset.
questions.revision: Keyset pagination on (createdAt, id), opaque validated cursor, limit plus one to detect a next page, bounded limit, and a 400 for tampered cursors.
followUps: When is offset pagination acceptable?
How would you paginate a result set merged from two sources?
How does the Relay connection spec model this?

questions.title: Fix a GraphQL N+1 problem with DataLoader
questions.quick: The N+1 appears because the Post.author resolver runs a query per post. I would create a DataLoader per request, in the GraphQL context, whose batch function receives all author IDs collected in one tick, runs a single IN query, and returns results in exactly the same order as the keys, with null or an error for missing ones. The resolver just calls loader.load. Per-request scope matters so the cache cannot leak data between users.
questions.revision: Create DataLoaders per request in context; the batch function takes all keys, does one query, and returns results aligned to key order.
followUps: Why must loaders be per request?
What does the batch function do if a key is missing?
How does DataLoader know when to dispatch a batch?

questions.title: Build useDebouncedValue and a race-safe useFetch hook
questions.quick: useDebouncedValue keeps a copy of the value in state and updates it from a timeout that the effect cleanup cancels, so only the last value within the delay wins. useFetch creates an AbortController per effect run, aborts it in cleanup, and ignores any result whose signal is aborted. That prevents an older, slower response overwriting a newer one and prevents state updates after unmount. I model state as a discriminated union rather than separate booleans.
questions.revision: Debounce with a cleanup-cancelled timeout; fetch with a per-effect AbortController, ignore aborted results, and model state as a discriminated union.
followUps: Why does Strict Mode run effects twice and how does this hook survive it?
What is the difference between debouncing the value and debouncing the callback?
Why use a discriminated union?

questions.title: Redux Toolkit slice with createAsyncThunk and memoised selectors
questions.quick: I would define a todos slice with status, error and filter fields. A createAsyncThunk fetches items, passes the thunk's abort signal to fetch, and uses rejectWithValue for HTTP errors so the reducer gets a typed message. extraReducers handle pending, fulfilled and rejected. Derived data, like the filtered list, lives in a createSelector so it only recomputes when its inputs change. I would test with a real store and a mocked fetch.
questions.revision: Slice with status and error, a typed thunk using the abort signal and rejectWithValue, extraReducers for lifecycle actions, and createSelector for derived lists.
followUps: Why is `createSelector` needed here?
What does `rejectWithValue` give you over throwing?
How do you prevent duplicate in-flight requests?

questions.title: Optimise a slow React list with memoisation and windowing
questions.quick: First I would measure with the React Profiler to find what re-renders and why. Typical fixes: memoise the row component, keep its props referentially stable with useCallback and functional state updates, and avoid creating new objects in render. If the list is thousands of rows, memoisation is not enough, so I would window it: render only the rows in the viewport plus overscan, positioned absolutely inside a spacer of full height. In production I would use a library like TanStack Virtual.
questions.revision: Profile first; memoise rows with stable props; for thousands of rows render only the visible window plus overscan inside a full-height spacer.
followUps: Why does `memo` fail if you pass an inline arrow function?
What is overscan for?
How would you diagnose re-renders without guessing?

questions.title: Apollo Client query, mutation and cache update
questions.quick: I would write a todos query with useQuery and an addTodo mutation with useMutation. The mutation returns the new object including its id and __typename, so Apollo can normalise it. Instead of refetching the whole list, I update the cached query in the update function using cache.updateQuery, and add an optimisticResponse so the UI changes instantly and rolls back on error. I handle loading and error states explicitly.
questions.revision: Query with useQuery; mutation returns id and __typename; update the cached list via cache.updateQuery with an optimisticResponse; handle loading and error.
followUps: What does normalisation do?
Why is `__typename` required in the optimistic response?
When would you prefer refetching over a manual cache update?

questions.title: Write React Testing Library tests for an async search
questions.quick: I would test behaviour the way a user experiences it. Render the component with a fake search function, type with userEvent, and use findBy queries that wait for the results. I would cover the happy path, an error shown with role alert, and the race condition: two requests in flight, the later one resolves first, then the earlier one resolves, and the screen must still show the later results. Deferred promises give me deterministic control without fake timers.
questions.revision: Test as a user: userEvent typing, findBy for async results, a role alert for errors, and a deferred-promise test proving stale responses are ignored.
followUps: Why query by role and label instead of test id?
What causes act warnings and how do you fix them?
How do you test a component that uses `useFetch`?

questions.title: Build an accessible signup form in React
questions.quick: I would use real labels tied to inputs, noValidate with my own validation so error messages are consistent, and per-field errors linked with aria-describedby plus aria-invalid. On a failed submit I show an error summary with links or a heading and move focus to it so screen reader users hear it immediately. Buttons disable only during submission and say so. The tests assert roles, names, focus and aria attributes rather than markup.
questions.revision: Real labels, aria-invalid and aria-describedby per field, an error summary that receives focus after a failed submit, and tests on roles and focus.
followUps: Why not use the `required` attribute alone?
When do you use `aria-live` versus moving focus?
How do you test accessibility automatically and what does that miss?

questions.title: Authentication and role-based authorisation middleware
questions.quick: I would split authentication from authorisation. The authenticate middleware extracts the bearer token, verifies it with an injected verifier, which in production wraps jose jwtVerify against the issuer's JWKS with fixed algorithms, issuer and audience, then stores a minimal user object in res.locals. A separate requireRole guard checks the roles claim and returns 403 when the user is known but not allowed, 401 when unauthenticated. Injection keeps tests free of real keys.
questions.revision: Verify the token with pinned issuer, audience and algorithms; keep authentication and the role guard separate; 401 for missing or bad tokens, 403 for insufficient role.
followUps: Why 401 versus 403?
What attacks do pinned algorithms prevent?
Where do you keep authorisation decisions: gateway, service or both?

questions.title: Cache-aside with TTL and cache stampede protection
questions.quick: I would implement cache-aside: check the cache, on a miss call the loader and store the result with a TTL. To stop a stampede, I keep a map of in-flight promises per key so concurrent misses share one loader call. I add small random jitter to expiry so many keys do not expire together. Failures are not cached, and invalidate removes a key after writes. In a multi-instance deployment the same idea needs a distributed lock or request coalescing in Redis.
questions.revision: Cache-aside with TTL, a per-key in-flight promise map so concurrent misses share one load, TTL jitter, failures not cached, explicit invalidation.
followUps: What causes a cache stampede?
Why add jitter to TTL?
Cache-aside versus write-through: when each?

diagrams.title: Cache-aside with request coalescing
diagrams.alt: A request checks the cache. A hit returns immediately. A miss checks the in-flight map; if a load is already running the request waits for it, otherwise it calls the loader, stores the value with a jittered TTL and releases the waiting requests.

questions.title: Idempotent order creation with an idempotency key
questions.quick: I would require an Idempotency-Key header and keep a table with the key as a unique primary key, a hash of the request payload, a status and the stored response. The first request inserts the row, which the unique constraint makes atomic, then creates the order and stores the response. A repeat with the same key and payload returns the stored response; the same key with a different payload is a 422; a repeat while the first is still running is a 409. On failure I release the key so the client can retry.
questions.revision: Unique-keyed idempotency record with payload hash and status: first insert wins, replays return the stored response, mismatched payload gives 422, in-progress gives 409.
followUps: Why is a unique constraint better than a read-then-write check?
What should happen when the first attempt failed with a 500?
How long should keys be retained?

diagrams.title: Idempotency key decision flow
diagrams.alt: An order request inserts its idempotency key. If the insert succeeds the order is created and the response stored. If the key exists with a different payload hash the request is rejected with 422. If it exists and is completed the stored response is returned. If it exists and is still in progress the request gets 409.

questions.title: Retry with exponential backoff and full jitter
questions.quick: I would write a retry helper with a maximum attempt count, exponential delay capped at a ceiling, and full jitter, meaning a random delay between zero and the cap, which spreads retries from many clients so they do not synchronise. A shouldRetry predicate restricts retries to transient errors such as network failures, 429 and 5xx. The sleep respects an AbortSignal, and sleep and random are injectable so tests are instant and deterministic.
questions.revision: Capped exponential delay with full jitter, a transient-error predicate, an abortable sleep, and injectable sleep and random for deterministic tests.
followUps: Why full jitter rather than a fixed delay?
Which HTTP statuses are safe to retry?
What is retry amplification?

questions.title: Implement a circuit breaker
questions.quick: I would implement the three-state machine. Closed counts consecutive failures; at the threshold it opens and rejects calls immediately with a CircuitOpenError, protecting the failing dependency and freeing callers quickly. After a reset timeout it moves to half-open and lets exactly one probe through; success closes the circuit, failure reopens it. Time is injected for tests, and I would expose state for metrics. Real systems often use a rolling failure rate rather than a simple count.
questions.revision: Closed counts failures, open fails fast, half-open allows one probe after a reset timeout; success closes, failure reopens. Inject time for tests.
followUps: Circuit breaker versus retry: how do they interact?
What should callers return while open?
Why not share breaker state across instances?

diagrams.title: Circuit breaker states
diagrams.alt: The circuit starts closed and counts failures. When failures reach the threshold it opens and rejects calls. After the reset timeout it becomes half-open and allows one probe. A successful probe closes the circuit; a failed probe opens it again.

questions.title: Implement a token bucket rate limiter
questions.quick: A token bucket has a capacity and a refill rate. I store the token count and last refill timestamp, and compute refills lazily on each request from elapsed time rather than running a timer. A request removes a token if available, otherwise it is rejected with a retry-after estimate. Burst capacity is allowed up to the bucket size while the long-run rate is capped. Per-client limits use a Map keyed by API key or IP, and a distributed version moves the logic into a Redis Lua script.
questions.revision: Lazy refill from elapsed time, capacity for bursts, tryRemove returning boolean, and a retry-after estimate; per-key buckets, and Redis Lua when distributed.
followUps: Token bucket versus leaky bucket?
What goes wrong with fixed windows?
How do you rate limit by user behind a shared IP?

questions.title: Implement an LRU cache with O(1) get and set
questions.quick: In JavaScript the simplest correct answer uses a Map, which preserves insertion order. On get I delete and re-insert the key so it becomes the most recently used. On set I do the same, and if the size exceeds capacity I delete the first key from the iterator, which is the least recently used. Both operations are O(1). If the interviewer wants it without Map ordering, I would use a hash map plus a doubly linked list with sentinel nodes.
questions.revision: Use a Map's insertion order: delete and re-set on access, evict the first key when over capacity. O(1) get and set; mention the linked-list alternative.
followUps: Why is Map insertion order enough?
LRU versus LFU: when would each win?
How would you make it thread-safe in a worker-threads setup?

questions.title: Run async tasks with a concurrency limit (promise pool)
questions.quick: I would start up to limit worker loops. Each loop repeatedly claims the next index from a shared counter, awaits the task and writes the result into its slot in a pre-sized array, so output order matches input order. Promise.all over the workers resolves when the queue is drained. For fail-fast, a flag stops other workers claiming new items after an error. This avoids both unbounded Promise.all fan-out and a chunked approach that waits for the slowest item in each batch.
questions.revision: N worker loops pull indices from a shared counter and write results by index, giving bounded concurrency and ordered results; a failure flag stops new work.
followUps: Why not chunk the array and `Promise.all` each chunk?
What happens to in-flight tasks when one fails?
How is this related to backpressure?

questions.title: Typed event emitter for in-process pub/sub
questions.quick: I would define the contract as an event map type, such as order created with an order ID, and make the emitter generic over it, so on and emit are checked: unknown event names and wrong payloads fail at compile time. on returns an unsubscribe function. Emit snapshots the handlers, runs them with allSettled so one failing subscriber cannot block the others, and reports failures through an error callback. This is in-process only; durability needs a broker.
questions.revision: Generic over an event map so on and emit are type-checked; on returns an unsubscribe; emit isolates handler failures with allSettled and reports errors.
followUps: Why use an event map type instead of strings?
What are the failure semantics when a handler throws?
When does in-process pub/sub stop being enough?

questions.title: Write a safe graceful shutdown handler for a Node server
questions.quick: On SIGTERM or SIGINT I run shutdown once. First mark the instance as not ready so the load balancer stops sending traffic, then call server.close so in-flight requests finish, and close idle keep-alive connections. After the server has drained I close dependencies in reverse order of creation, such as queues, then database. A hard timeout, unref'd so it does not hold the process, forces exit code 1 if draining takes too long. Repeated signals are ignored.
questions.revision: Run once; fail readiness; stop accepting and drain with server.close and closeIdleConnections; close dependencies in reverse order; hard timeout forces exit.
followUps: Why not call `process.exit` immediately?
What does `server.close` actually wait for?
How does readiness differ from liveness during shutdown?

diagrams.title: Graceful shutdown sequence
diagrams.alt: On a termination signal the process marks itself not ready, stops accepting new connections, waits for in-flight requests to finish, closes dependencies in reverse order and exits with code zero. A timer forces exit with code one if draining takes too long.
